extracted.intended_audience: statesmen, legislators, political thinkers, and the politically engaged public (late-18th-century Britain)
extracted.subtask_description: Principled criteria for judging the justice, prudence, and policy of large-scale political reforms and revolutionary measures, especially concerning property, institutions, and legitimate authority. The page argues for preservation-with-improvement, gradual reform, and an evidence-based, humane temper in legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for justice as the primary public policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice itself is the great standing policy of civil society, and any eminent departure from it, under any circumstances, lies under the suspicion of being no policy at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy cannot legitimately override basic justice; large measures (e.g., confiscations) must be judged primarily by their justice, not merely by asserted utility. Anti-pattern: treating 'policy' as license for unjust acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid arbitrary retroactive degradation of established lawful modes of life
rubrics_metrics.description: When men are encouraged to go into a certain mode of life by the existing laws... it is unjust in legislature, by an arbitrary act, to offer a sudden violence to their minds and their feelings, forcibly to degrade them from their state and condition and to stigmatize with shame and infamy that character and those customs which before had been made the measure of their happiness and honor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislatures should not suddenly stigmatize or punish behavior that was previously lawful and respectable. Reforms that amount to abrupt moral or legal delegitimization of entire classes are unjust and tyrannical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public benefit must clearly outweigh injustice to justify radical measures
rubrics_metrics.description: If the injustice of the course pursued in France be clear, the policy of the measure... ought to be at least as evident and at least as important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any severe interference (confiscation, expulsion) requires evidence of commensurate public benefit; mere expediency is insufficient. Reforms must show clear, substantial public advantage to offset injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve-and-improve principle (Spartam nactus es; hanc exorna)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is something else than the mere alternative of absolute destruction or unreformed existence. 'Spartam nactus es; hanc exorna.' ... A disposition to preserve and an ability to improve, taken together, would be my standard of a statesman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good reformers should work with existing institutions' materials — keep useful parts and adapt them — rather than total abolition. The standard of a statesman is both preservation and improvement; rash destruction is vulgar and perilous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use existing institutional capacities as instruments of public good
rubrics_metrics.description: In the monastic institutions... were revenues with a public direction; there were men wholly set apart and dedicated to public purposes... implicit obedience stands in the place of freedom. ... These institutions are the products of enthusiasm; they are the instruments of wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and harness revenues, organizational discipline, and durable institutions as tools for public projects instead of destroying them. Anti-pattern: selling off institutional assets carelessly or converting them wastefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform should prefer adaptation over destroying social 'energies'
rubrics_metrics.description: To destroy any power growing wild from the rank productive force of the human mind is almost tantamount... to the destruction of the apparently active properties of bodies in the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions may contain latent useful forces; reformers should tame and adapt those energies rather than obliterate them. Consider long-term, systemic value before dismantling structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerate minor or tempered superstition if it serves social ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Superstition is the religion of feeble minds; and they must be tolerated in an intermixture of it... else you will deprive weak minds of a resource found necessary to the strongest. ... perhaps he would think the superstition which builds to be more tolerable than that which demolishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all religious or superstitious practices should be eradicated if they have social utility or provide resources to vulnerable people. Prioritize mitigation of harms rather than wholesale eradication; prefer forms that 'adorn' and 'endow' rather than those that 'plunder' or 'deform.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate economic consequences of property transfer and purchasers' character
rubrics_metrics.description: Before the inconveniences are incurred... we ought to have some rational assurance that the purchasers of the confiscated property will be in a considerable degree more laborious, more virtuous, more sober... than the old possessors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering confiscation and sale, assess who will acquire property and whether their spending and stewardship will better serve industry, morals, and the public good. Anti-pattern: assuming purchasers will automatically be improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of long-term cultural and scientific expenditures
rubrics_metrics.description: Does not the sweat of the mason and carpenter... flow as pleasantly and as salubriously in the construction and repair of the majestic edifices of religion... as in the painted booths and sordid sties of vice and luxury? ... great collections of ancient records, medals, and coins... paintings and statues... collections of the specimens of nature...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expenditures on libraries, monuments, scientific collections, and durable cultural goods are legitimate and often superior uses of surplus product compared with ephemeral luxury; preserve such public-oriented expenditures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate/established bodies are amenable to public direction and reform
rubrics_metrics.description: I always consider corporate bodies... to be much more susceptible of a public direction by the power of the state, in the use of their property and in the regulation of modes and habits of life in their members, than private citizens ever can be or, perhaps, ought to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer reform measures that direct or repurpose corporate bodies rather than dispossessing them outright; the state can steer established entities toward public ends more effectively than it can micro-manage many scattered individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some tenure by duty-bound holders is socially useful
rubrics_metrics.description: Can any philosophic spoiler undertake to demonstrate the positive or the comparative evil of having a certain, and that too a large, portion of landed property passing in succession through persons whose title to it is... piety, morals, and learning... a property which, by its destination... gives to the noblest families renovation and support, to the lowest the means of dignity and elevation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that land held by persons with duties (bishops, canons, etc.) can have social advantages — decorum, hospitality, charity — and that tenure tied to duties is not necessarily bad for the commonwealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy and prescription are required for new governments
rubrics_metrics.description: I can never consider this Assembly as anything else than a voluntary association of men who have availed themselves of circumstances to seize upon the power of the state... They do not hold the authority they exercise under any constitutional law of the state. The most considerable of their acts have not been done by great majorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New governing bodies must show legal or necessity-based justification and, with time ('prescription'), acquire legitimacy. Acts done without constitutional authority or broad assent deserve scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish methods of obtaining power from competence to govern
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything which they have done, or continue to do, in order to obtain and keep their power is by the most common arts... But in all the regulations relative to the public good, the spirit has been the very reverse of this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize the techniques leaders use to seize power separately from the suitability of their policies; success in political maneuvering does not imply skill in governance or prudence in public affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: True skill in reform requires confronting and working through difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulty is a severe instructor... This inability to wrestle with difficulty which has obliged the arbitrary Assembly of France to commence their schemes of reform with abolition and total destruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governing wisdom is shown by engagement with complexities, not by opting for simplistic destructive solutions. Avoid leaders who escape difficulty through radical sweeping measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer slow, empirical, incremental reform over rapid experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: By a slow but well-sustained progress the effect of each step is watched; the good or ill success of the first gives light to us in the second; and so, from light to light, we are conducted with safety through the whole series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use time and staged interventions as tools: monitor, learn, and adapt. Rapid wholesale reforms risk unforeseen harms; circumspection and caution are virtues in political engineering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political arrangement is a social work requiring social means
rubrics_metrics.description: Political arrangement, as it is a work for social ends, is to be only wrought by social means. There mind must conspire with mind. Time is required to produce that union of minds which alone can produce all the good we aim at.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation and constitutional change should be achieved through deliberation, consensus-building, and inclusive consultation, not by unilateral fiat or isolated theorizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid basing policy solely on untried speculative theories
rubrics_metrics.description: They abandon the dearest interests of the public to those loose theories to which none of them would choose to trust the slightest of his private concerns... their schemes have nothing in experience to prove their tendency beneficial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reforms should be grounded in practice and experience; caution against grand theoretical schemes untested by real-world evidence. Anti-pattern: trusting abstract paradoxes or rhetorical marvels as blueprints for public policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of reformers whose disposition is to 'pull everything in pieces'
rubrics_metrics.description: By hating vices too much, they come to love men too little. From hence arises the complexional disposition of some of your guides to pull everything in pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique those motivated by contempt rather than constructive care; successful reformers should combine critique with appreciation of human frailty and the capacity to improve institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test proposals by comparing old and new possessors' moral and economic effects
rubrics_metrics.description: A sober legislator would carefully compare the possessor whom he was recommended to expel with the stranger who was proposed to fill his place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before displacing existing holders of property or office, evaluate whether successors will manage resources better and whether the transition will serve public ends; avoid assuming novelty equals improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject impatience and taste for the marvelous as legislative virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: That the marvelous in life, in manners, in characters... that species of the marvelous which might still be produced... I believe that were Rousseau alive... he would be shocked at the practical frenzy of his scholars, who in their paradoxes are servile imitators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislators should not be swayed by rhetorical novelty or sensational schemes. Preference should be given to sober judgment over dazzling but untested proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose systems to reconcile competing principles rather than simplify at expense of balance
rubrics_metrics.description: We compensate, we reconcile, we balance. We are enabled to unite into a consistent whole the various anomalies and contending principles that are found in the minds and affairs of men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good constitutional design aims for composition and balance, acknowledging trade-offs and reconciling competing interests rather than pursuing one-dimensional simplicity that sacrifices important goods.
